title: The fox in the town
text: The red fox arrived in British cities within living memory, its {{1}} (EXPAND) tracking the semi-detached suburbs of the 1930s. Today it is a permanent urban institution: researchers in Bristol have followed marked animals for decades, producing the most {{2}} (COMPREHEND) picture of any urban wild mammal anywhere. The science punctures several tabloid myths. City foxes are not {{3}} (MAIN) bin-raiders — studies of diet find they eat mostly earthworms, beetles and rodents — and they are not pack hunters: several foxes together usually means a mother with her grown {{4}} (CUB) from previous years. Nor are numbers exploding. Despite headlines, the urban population has stayed broadly flat for decades, and talk of an {{5}} (EXPLODE) has no statistical basis. City life has genuine costs, of course: traffic kills more foxes than anything else, and mange, a mite-borne disease that leaves its victims {{6}} (MISERY), sweeps periodically through the population. Attitudes, meanwhile, remain broadly friendly. Surveys repeatedly find that most urban residents regard the fox with {{7}} (TOLERATE) or outright affection, and complaints peak only during the mating season's notorious screams. The species' success, biologists suggest, is ultimately a tribute to its {{8}} (ADAPT): a wild predator that learned, better than almost any other, to live alongside us.

'her grown cubs from previous years' — plural pinned by 'previous years'.

'a tribute to its adaptability' — the quality noun from adapt.
